meta_description: The native Mac password manager for Vaultwarden and Bitwarden. Every feature free to try, nothing locked; {price} once, for life, if it stays.
meta_title: Triwarden — the native Mac password manager for Vaultwarden & Bitwarden
meta_og_image_alt: The Triwarden app icon, a three-ring dial around a keyhole
hero_eyebrow: {version} for macOS 26 · every feature free to try
hero_lede: The Mac password manager your Vaultwarden deserves. Native, quick, and yours to try for as long as you like — nothing locked, no trial clock.
languages_label: Languages: English, Traditional Chinese (Taiwan), Traditional Chinese (Hong Kong), Simplified Chinese, Japanese
screens_lede: SwiftUI all the way down: system materials, light and dark, full keyboard control and VoiceOver. Not a web page in a frame.
alt_vault: The vault: sidebar, item list, and a GitHub login with its password, live one-time code, passkey and attachments
alt_codes: A grid of one-time codes, each with a countdown ring
alt_watchtower: Watchtower: a score, the logins exposed in breaches and the reused passwords, each with Change on Site
alt_palette: The command palette over the vault, searching “git”: GitHub first with its live code, then GitLab, Gitea and more
alt_generator: The generator with length, character sets and history
alt_menubar: The menu bar panel: the page’s login, favorites with live codes, quick actions and the generator
alt_signin: Signing in to a self-hosted Vaultwarden server
cap_vault: Every item type, folders, favorites, passkeys and attachments, in one quiet window.
cap_codes: Every one-time code at a glance, each with its countdown ring. Click to copy.
cap_watchtower: A score, the passwords that need you, and a button to each site’s change-password page.
cap_palette: Search everything, run anything. ⌘K in the window, ⇧⌘Space from anywhere.
cap_generator: Passwords, passphrases and usernames, with a history of what you used.
cap_menubar: The page you’re on, your favorites and their codes, one click from any app.
cap_signin: Self-hosted, Bitwarden US or Bitwarden EU — pick one and sign in.
cap_lock: The lock: a vault door that turns as you type, and takes itself apart when you’re in.
palette_p1: Press {shortcut} over Safari, Chrome or any app and the palette already has that site’s login on top. Hit return and Triwarden types it in — auto-type, without the setup.
palette_p2: In the window it’s {shortcut}: every item and every command, a few keystrokes away.
mac_title_1: Not a website in a box.
row_menubar_body: The login for the page you’re on, your favorites with live codes, quick actions and the generator — all in the menu bar.
row_ssh_title: Your SSH keys, guarded by Touch ID.
row_ssh_body: Keep keys in the vault, not in {path}. Triwarden answers {ssh} and signs your git commits, one tap at a time.
row_cli_body: {tw} on the command line, Shortcuts and App Intents, a Safari extension and a Chrome native host. Reading the vault always asks for Touch ID.
security_lede: Zero-knowledge encryption, a hardware-backed unlock and end-to-end sync. Each ring of the dial is one lock on your vault, and all three have to line up before it opens.
lock1_body: Your master password never leaves the Mac. Keys are derived on-device with PBKDF2 or Argon2id, and the server only ever stores ciphertext it can’t read.
lock2_body: One press of Touch ID unlocks every account at once. Keys live in the Keychain, guarded by the Secure Enclave — not in a file, not in memory longer than they need to be.
lock3_body: Self-host Vaultwarden, or use Bitwarden cloud in the US or EU. Everything is encrypted before it syncs — live over WebSocket, and readable offline.
lock4_title: All three line up. The vault opens.
lock4_body: On the lock screen the rings turn as you type. When the last one lands in line, the door takes itself apart.
gen_body: Passwords, passphrases from the EFF wordlist, and usernames — with a history, so nothing you generated is ever lost.
wt_p1: Breached, reused and weak passwords, sites still on http://, and two-step logins you haven’t turned on — each with a button to that site’s change-password page.
wt_p2: Breach checks use Have I Been Pwned’s k-anonymity: five characters of a hash leave your Mac, never the password.
more_autofill_b: System AutoFill for passwords, passkeys and one-time codes in Safari, Chrome and apps. A google.com login fills on youtube.com.
more_send_b: Share text or a file through an encrypted link. Edit it later; the link stays the same.
more_emergency_b: Trusted contacts can view or take over your vault after a wait you choose.
more_import_b: 1Password, LastPass, KeePass, Bitwarden, Proton Pass, Dashlane, Apple Passwords, Chrome, Firefox.
more_accounts_b: Self-hosted and cloud side by side. One Touch ID unlocks them all.
more_orgs_b: Shared vaults with nested shared folders. Show one vault, several or all of them; event logs for admins.
more_offline_b: Read everything from the encrypted cache while the server is away.
more_clipboard_b: Copied secrets clear themselves, with a countdown in the footer.
more_history_b: When it changed, and every password it had before.
more_bulk_b: ⌘-click, ⇧-click or ⌘A, then move, archive or trash them in one go.
more_2fa_b: Authenticator app, email, recovery codes, and approving sign-ins from your other devices.
more_lang_b: English, 繁體中文 (台灣 · 香港), 简体中文 and 日本語.
more_unlock_b: One touch unlocks every account; a lock timeout for each, or log out instead of lock.
more_a11y_b: VoiceOver, full keyboard control, Increase Contrast and Reduce Motion.
price_lede: Try everything for as long as you like. If Triwarden earns its place on your Mac, buy it once — no subscription, no renewal date, every future update included.
perk_life: Yours for life — one payment, forever
perk_pay: Card, Alipay, WeChat Pay or PayPal
price_reminder: Until then, official builds show a gentle reminder at most once a week, and once after each update. That’s all.
how1_b: Get the signed app from GitHub, or install it with Homebrew.
how2_b: No trial clock, nothing greyed out. Take a week or a year.
how3_b: If it earns its place, {price} through Lemon Squeezy. Paste the key and you’re done.
how4_b: Every update after that is yours too. There’s nothing to renew.
honest1_b: No trial clock and nothing greyed out. Use every feature until you decide.
honest2_b: Registering a receipt key asks Lemon Squeezy once, then never again. Offline keys never leave your Mac. Nothing phones home.
honest3_b: The source is GPL-3.0. Clone it, run make, and it’s yours — free, always.
faq1_q: Is anything locked until I pay?
faq1_a: No. Every feature works from the first launch, with no time limit. Unlicensed official builds show a gentle reminder at most once a week, and once after each update.
faq2_q: How many Macs does one license cover?
faq2_a: Every Mac you own — no device limit — for life, with every future update. It’s {price}, once; there’s nothing to renew.
faq3_a: Only once, and only if you choose to: registering a receipt key asks Lemon Squeezy to confirm it. After that nothing in the app contacts anyone about licensing. Offline license keys never leave your Mac.
faq4_q: Which servers does it work with?
faq4_a: Self-hosted Vaultwarden, and Bitwarden cloud in the US and EU — several accounts at once, all unlocked with one Touch ID.
faq5_q: Can I build it from source?
faq5_a: Yes. Triwarden is free software under the GPL-3.0; building it yourself is always free. Forks need their own name and icon.
faq6_a: Through Lemon Squeezy, by card, Alipay, WeChat Pay or PayPal.
faq7_a: Contact method: email — {email}. Write there for purchase or product questions. For bugs, open a GitHub issue; for security reports, see Security.
close_body: Download it free and take your time. If it stays, it’s {price} — once, for life, on every Mac you own.
close_requires: Requires macOS 26 or later. Updates itself; Homebrew keeps the cask current.
foot_disclaimer: Not affiliated with Bitwarden, Inc. or the Vaultwarden project. Bitwarden is a trademark of Bitwarden, Inc.
row_autotype_title: Types your login into any app.
row_autotype_body: KeePass-style auto-type, built in. Over any page or app, the palette puts its logins first and Return types the username and password for you. Or skip the palette: {shortcut} fills the page you’re on.
kt_submit: Add to any of these to submit too
kt_global: From anywhere: fill the page or app you’re in
alt_search: Searching “north” across My vault and the Northwind shared vault, with filter chips under the field
cap_search: One search over every vault, with filters that stay on between launches.
search_body: Search your own vault and every shared vault at once, and narrow it with filters that stay on: type a token like {tokens}, or pick one from the menu. Chips show what’s on; Esc takes them off.
speed_note: Download size of the latest release. Memory measured with make bench on an Apple M4 Pro with a 200+ item vault; it varies by Mac.
more_keys_b: Help › Keyboard Shortcuts (⌘/) lists every key — in the window, the palette and system-wide.
g_meta: How to use Triwarden's SSH agent: keys in your vault for ssh and git, approved with Touch ID or your Mac password.
g_lede: Triwarden can answer ssh and git the way ssh-agent does, from SSH Key items in your vault. The private key never leaves the app, and every signature asks you first.
g_flow_caption: ssh asks the agent to sign. Triwarden asks you — Touch ID or your Mac password — signs inside the app, and sends back only the signature.
g_s1_b: Open Triwarden › Settings › Developer and switch on Use Triwarden as SSH agent. It runs while the app is open and offers keys only while your vault is unlocked.
g_s2_b: Make a new SSH Key item. Press Generate Ed25519 Key for a fresh one, or paste a private key you already have — an unencrypted OpenSSH key (-----BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY-----). Ed25519, ECDSA (P-256, P-384, P-521) and RSA all work, and SSH keys saved by other Bitwarden apps show up too.
g_s2_tip: Key has a passphrase? The agent can’t use encrypted keys. Make an unencrypted copy, paste it into the item, then delete the copy — the vault keeps it encrypted from then on.
g_s3_b: Add the agent to ~/.ssh/config — Settings › Developer › SSH setup has a Copy button with your own path filled in. Or set it for a single shell.
g_s3_note: Prefer the config file: apps opened from the Dock (VS Code, Tower, Fork, Xcode) don’t see your shell’s variables, but every ssh reads the config.
g_s4_b: ssh-add -L lists the public keys the agent offers. Nothing there? See the fixes below.
g_c1_b: Copy the item’s public key into GitHub › Settings › SSH and GPG keys as an Authentication key (GitLab: User settings › SSH keys). Then test it:
g_c2_b: Put the public key in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server, then ssh in as usual. Only signatures go over the wire.
g_c3_b: On the key’s page, Git signing › Copy Setup gives you these three lines. Add the same public key to GitHub as a Signing key and your commits show Verified.
g_c3_note: To check signatures locally too, list the keys you trust:
g_c4_b: With many keys, a server can stop at “Too many authentication failures” before it reaches the right one. Save that key’s public half to a file and pin it to the host:
g_c5_b: Rather keep another agent for everything else? Use Triwarden for named hosts only:
g_c6_b: VS Code, Tower, Fork, Xcode and anything else that runs the system’s ssh pick up ~/.ssh/config, so they work once step 3 is done. The approval appears for them the same way.
g_appr_b: Each request names the program and the key — “allow ssh to sign with the SSH key GitHub”. Choose how often to be asked in Settings › Developer › Ask before signing:
g_appr_o1_b: the default: one prompt per signature
g_appr_o2_b: handy for a burst of git fetches
g_appr_o3_b: for long sessions; locking forgets it
g_appr_nomac: No Touch ID — a Mac mini, a Mac Studio, a closed lid? macOS asks for your Mac password instead, and Deny refuses. Settings › Developer lists the last few requests, allowed or denied.
g_sec_1: The private key stays in Triwarden; ssh and git only ever get signatures.
g_sec_2: Locked vault, no keys: the agent offers nothing until you unlock, and locking forgets every remembered approval.
g_sec_3: Archived and deleted items are never offered.
g_tr1_a: The vault is locked, the agent is off, there are no SSH Key items, or the key in the item has a passphrase (encrypted keys aren’t offered).
g_tr2_q: “Could not open a connection to your authentication agent”
g_tr2_a: This shell doesn’t know where the agent is. Add the IdentityAgent line to ~/.ssh/config, or run the export from step 3 in that shell.
g_tr3_a: The request was denied, or the prompt was left until it timed out. Run the command again and approve.
g_tr4_a: The server gave up before reaching the right key. Pin the key to the host (Several keys, above).
g_cta_b: Free to try with every feature, the SSH agent included.
